titleStmt.title: A Pre-emptive Transaction Scheduling Protocol for Controlling Priority Inversion

analytic.title: A Pre-emptive Transaction Scheduling Protocol for Controlling Priority Inversion

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: Hard real-time database systems (RTDBS) must provide a guarantee that real-time transactions meet their deadlines. To preserve data consistency, hard RTDBS require concurrency control protocols to synchronize transactions to access the shared data. Transaction blocking enforced by concurrency control protocols leads to the priority inversion problem that violates the princple of priority-based scheduling and degrades system schedulability.

Moreover, this blocking deluy due to priority inversion can be unbounded, which is unacceptable in hard real-time applications. Some priority ceiling protocols have been proposed to control priority inversion. However, they suffer from the problem of unnecessary transaction blockings due to their conservatism of scheduling transactions to access the shared data We propose a new transaction scheduling protocol that exploits the semantics of transaction operations to enhance transaction preemptability. It can avoid some unnecessary transaction blockings and provide better worst-case scheduling conditions for a transaction set compared to other protocols.

div.head: Introduction
div.p: Hard read-time database systems (RTDBS) must provide a guarantee that real-time transactions meet their deadlines [9]. Hard RTDBS require concurrency control protocols to synchronize transactions to access the shared data to ensure serializable executions of transactions [l]. An important problem that arises in the priority-based scheduling in real-time systems is the impact of transaction blocking enforced by concurrency control protocols. To preserve data consistency, transactions are normally blocked if they access the shared data in conflicting mode. Priority inversion occurs when a high-priority transaction is blocked while a lower priority transaction has locked the shared data item which the higher priority transaction attempts to lock [SI. Priority inversion should be minimised as it degrades system schedulability. Unfortunately, this blocking time can be indefinitely long which is unacceptable in hard realtime applications.

To cope with the priority inversion problem, a class of priority ceiling protocols [2,3,10] have been proposed to integrate priority-based scheduling and concurrency control protocols using the notion of priority ceiling. A priority ceiling is defined for each resource. The priority ceiling of a resource is the highest priority task that may access the resource. These protocols were basically developed for the synchronization of tasks on exclusive access to the shared resources in real-time systems. These protocols have two important properties : single-blocking and deadlock-free. Single-blocking means that a task blocking delay due to priority inversion is bounded by at most the duration of a single critical section. However, these protocols cannot directly be applied to RTDBS because they cannot guarantee the serializable executions of real-time transactions. Sha et al. [ l l ] extended the original priority ceiling protocol [ 101 in hard RTDBS. They proposed the read-write priority ceiling protocol (RW-PCP) which combined two phase locking (2PL) with PCP.

They assigned two different priority ceilings to each data item for read and write operation semantics of transactions. Due to the priority inheritance mechanism, RW-PCP does not need explicitly to check for readwrite operation conflicts. RW-PCP guarantees that a transaction can be blocked by at most a single lower priority transaction. RW-PCP can also avoid deadlocks. However, RW-PCP suffers from the problem of unnecessary transaction blockings due to its conservatism of scheduling transactions to access the shared data.

In this paper, we investigate the problem of the unnecessary transaction blockings inherent in some priority ceiling protocols [7,11] for hard RTDBS and propose a new transaction scheduling protocol that exploits the semantics of transaction operations to enhance transaction preemptability so that the transaction blocking delay due to priority inversion can be minimized.

The remainder of this paper is organised as follows: Section 2 discusses the problem of unnecessary transaction blockings inherent in some priority ceiling protocols. In Section 3, we introduces the basic concept of the new protocol. We propose a new priority ceiling protocol in Section 4. A working example is given to illustrate the superiority of the new protocol over RW-PCP. Proofs of correctness and properties are given in Section 6 . We provide the schedulability analysis using the new protocol in Section 7 and conclude in Section 8.

In RW-PCP, T, has to wait until T, finishes its execution and releases all its locks. TI is blocked for data consistency requirement because RW-PCP uses 2PL. However, if we assume the update-in-workspace model [ l ] in which transactions defer their updates at the end of their executions, TI will not have to be blocked. In this model, before a transaction commits, it reads and updates data items only in its private workspace and then data items are written into the database only upon successful commit. Since the serialization order among transactions will only be fixed at the commitment of transactions, it provides a greater flexibility in resolving data conflicts and in determining the serialization order. In fact, some past work on realtime concurrency control adopted this model [4,5,13].

div.head: Unnecessary Transaction Blocking 3 Basic Concept of the New Protocol
div.p: Although we use the Readwrite Priority Ceiling Protocol (RW-PCP) [ 113 as an example to illustrate the problem of unnecessary transaction blockings, the similar argument can also be applied to other priority ceiling protocols for hard RTDBS [7]. In RW-PCP, a transaction Ti cannot read-lock or write-lock a data item unless its priority is higher than the highest priority ceiling of all data items locked by transactions other than Ti. Consider the following example: In this section, we examine the ways of enhancing the capabilities of high priority transactions to preempt lower priority transactions to avoid transaction blocking as far as the data consistency can still be preserved.

We assume the update-in-workspace transaction model. Although some previous work [ 121 took the approach of restarting transactions to resolving data conflict among transactions, it complicates system schedulability analysis. Thus, we assume that a transaction pre-emption will not entail transaction restarts.

div.head: Pre-emption Conditions
div.p: In priority-based scheduling, a lower priority transaction T, may block a higher priority transaction TH only when it has accessed a data item before TH attempts to access it in the incompatible mode. Suppose T, has accessed a data item x. We consider three possible cases of data conflicts in which TH will be blocked in other protocols [7,11] and analyse whether TH is allowed to pre-empt TL under the requirement of no transactions restarts. Let Read,(x) and Write,(x) denote transaction T, reads and writes data item x respectively.

In this case, TH can pre-empt TL provided that TH must commit before TL. If TL commits first after T, pre-empts TL, TL's write will invalidate TH's read. In that case, TH has to be restarted and it is forbidden in our new protocol. To ensure that TH commits before TL, we must make sure that TH does not have any other data conflicts either directly or indirectly with TL in which cases, TH will be blocked. In fact, the serialization order between TL and TH has to be TL -+ T,. In this case, it precludes TH from pre-empting TL.

These two write operations are blind write operations. TH can pre-empt TL because whether TH or TL commits first will not compromise the data consistency and will not restart one of them. Thus, the serialization order between TL and TH can be either TL -+ T, or TH + TL depending on which transaction commits first.

However, in the example 2, we show that with these write-write conflicts, even if TL and TH have other prior data conflicts, no constraint on the serialization order is induced and the shared data consistency will not be compromised.

div.head: Priority Ceiling Control
div.p: We employ a priority ceiling mechanism to block lower priority transactions earlier for the singleblocking property.

In most priority ceiling protocols [7,11], two types of priority ceilings are defined for each data item for the semantics of read and write operations of transactions. The use of priority ceilings is to block the operations of lower priority transactions that may conflict and block that of higher priority transactions.

In our new protocol, only one priority ceiling is needed for each data item although we also consider the semantics of transaction read/write operations. As discussed in Section 3.1, the transaction's write operations are pre-emptable operations. That is, under no circumstances will they block the readwrite operations of higher priority transactions. However, the read operations may block the write operations of higher priority transactions. Based on this observation, it is not necessary to define a priority ceiling to control the write operations. Thus, only a priority ceiling, called write priority ceiling, is needed to control the read operations.

div.head: A New Priority Ceiling Protocol
div.p: We assume that the system has a single processor with the whole database residing on the main memory and that all transactions under the update-in-workspace model are periodic transactions with rate monotonic priority assignment [6]. That is, a transaction with a shorter period is assigned a higher priority and the deadline of a transaction is at the end of its period. The priorities of transactions are of a total order. This initial priority of a transaction is called the original priority. Transactions are assigned to the processor based on their current running priorities that are initially equal to their original priorities. If a transaction blocks a higher priority transaction, its running priority will inherit that of the higher priority transaction. The transaction with the highest running priority ready to execute is scheduled to run on the processor. Before a transaction can read or write a data item x, it must first obtain read or write lock on the data item x respectively. All the locks will only be released after the commitment of a transaction.

Each data item x is assigned a write priority ceiling WPC(x) that is the priority of the highest priority transactions that may write x. Note that WPC(x) will come into effect only if x is read-locked by transactions. However, write operations will not make WPC(x) to take effect. Let PI denote the priority of transaction TI and SPC, denotes the system priority ceiling with respect to TI that is the highest WPC(x) among all the data items read-locked by transactions other than TI. Now, we define the mechanism of the new priority ceiling protocol. Transaction T, is allowed to read-lock or write-lock a data item x if one of the following two concurrency control rules is true.

In this section, we first prove the correctness of the new protocol, i.e. it ensures serializable executions of transactions. Then we also prove the two important properties: the single-blocking and deadlock-free, which a good priority ceiling protocol should have. For the correctness of the new protocol, we prove that all histories, H, produced by the new protocol cannot have a cycle in the serialization graph, SG(H) [I]. Lemma 1 : I f a transaction successfilly commits, it will not have write-read conjlicts with the currently running transactions. Proof : Suppose T, has write-read conflicts with a currently running transaction T,. The condition, Writeset, n DataRead, st 0, is sufficient to prevent TH from pre-empting T,. In this case, TH would be blocked and would not commit before T,, which contradicts our assumption. Hence, the Lemma follows.
Theorem 2 : If H is a history produced by the new protocol, then H is serializable.

Hence, pJ(x) and y,(x) are either ReadJ(x) and Write,(x) or WriteJ(x) and Read,(x). By Lemma 1, pJ(x) and y,(x) should be ReadJ(x) and Write,(x) respectively. We claim that the commitment of TJ precedes that of TI. For suppose TI was committed first. At the time TI commits, Write,(x) must have been processed by the system; hence Write,(x) precedes ReadJ(x) and conflicts with it. Since TJ is currently executing, T, cannot commit as it violates Lemma 1. It is contrary to our assumption that TI is committed before TJ in H.

In the following, we prove the deadlock-free property. To have a deadlock, there must be a circularwait situation. In the circular wait situation, each transaction in the cycle has locked some data items while waiting to lock a data item which is being locked by another transaction. In the new protocol, write operations are pre-emptable operations. Hence, by Lemma 3, a transaction can block other transactions only if it has read-locked at least a data item.

By Lemma 4, no lower priority transaction can inherit a priority level greater than or equal to P,. It implies that no lower priority transaction can block TH or any other higher priority transaction. Moreover, in the priority-based scheduling, no arriving transaction with priority lower than PH can pre-empt TH. Thus, TH cannot be blocked by lower priority transactions before TH completes its execution.

For TH to read-lock a data item, if R2 is true, by Lemma 8, TH will not be blocked by TL until the end of '1,'s execution. Hence, a deadlock cannot occur. The Theorem follows.

div.head: Conclusions
div.p: Priority inversion problem arises when concurrency control protocols are adapted to prioritybased scheduling in hard real-time database systems. Some priority ceiling protocols [7,11] have been proposed to solve the priority inversion problem and provide the worst-case schedulability analysis. However, they are too conservative in scheduling transactions to access the shared data. As a result, some transaction blockings may be unnecessary, thus reducing the schedulability condition of a transaction set.

In this paper, we have proposed a new priority ceiling protocol that exploits the semantics of transaction operations to enhance transaction preemptability. The new protocol can solve the problem of unnecessary transaction blockings inherent in some other protocols.

We have proved its correctness. It has also the two important properties : the single-blocking and deadlock-free properties which are necessary for the schedulability analysis in hard real-time database systems. We have also presented better schedulability conditions for systems using the new protocol.
